{{short description|Exponential function of an exponential function}}
[[Image:Double Exponential Function.svg|right|thumb|320px|A double exponential function (red curve) compared to a single exponential function (blue curve).]]

A '''double exponential''' function is a [[Constant (mathematics)|constant]] raised to the power of an [[Exponentiation|exponential function]].  The general formula is <math>f(x) = a^{b^x}=a^{(b^x)}</math> (where {{math|''a'' > 1}} and {{math|''b'' > 1}}), which grows much more quickly than an exponential function. For example, if {{math|1=''a'' = ''b'' = 10}}:
*{{math|1=''f''(''x'') = 10{{sup|10{{sup|''x''}}}}}}
*{{math|1=''f''(0) = 10}}
*{{math|1=''f''(1) = 10{{sup|10}}}}
*{{math|1=''f''(2) = 10{{sup|100}} = [[googol]]}}
*{{math|1=''f''(3) = 10{{sup|1000}}}}
*{{math|1=''f''(100) = 10{{sup|10{{sup|100}}}} = [[googolplex]]}}.

[[Factorial]]s grow faster than exponential functions, but much more slowly than double exponential functions. However, [[tetration]] and the [[Ackermann function]] grow faster. See [[Big O notation]] for a comparison of the rate of growth of various functions.

The inverse of the double exponential function is the [[Logarithm#double logarithm|double logarithm]] {{math|log(log(''x''))}}. The complex double exponential function is [[Entire function|entire]], because it is the composition of two entire functions <math>f(x)=a^x=e^{x\ln a}</math> and <math>g(x)=b^x=e^{x\ln b}</math>.

==Double exponential sequences==

A sequence of positive integers (or real numbers) is said to have ''double exponential rate of growth'' if the function giving the {{mvar|n}}th term of the sequence is bounded above and below by double exponential functions of {{mvar|n}}.
Examples include
* The [[Fermat number]]s <math display="block">F(m) = 2^{2^m}+1</math>
* The harmonic primes: The primes {{mvar|p}}, in which the sequence {{math|1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + ⋯ + 1/''p''}} exceeds 0, 1, 2, 3, …{{pb}}The first few numbers, starting with 0, are 2, 5, 277, 5195977, ... {{OEIS|A016088}}
* The [[Double Mersenne number]]s <math display="block">MM(p) = 2^{2^p-1}-1</math>
* The elements of [[Sylvester's sequence]] {{OEIS|A000058}} <math display="block">s_n = \left\lfloor E^{2^{n+1}}+\frac12 \right\rfloor</math> where {{math|1=''E'' ≈ 1.264084735305302}} is [[Vardi's constant]] {{OEIS|A076393}}.
* The number of [[Arity|{{mvar|k}}-ary]] [[Boolean function]]s: <math display="block">2^{2^k}</math>
* The prime numbers 2, 11, 1361, ... {{OEIS|A051254}} <math display="block">a(n) = \left\lfloor A^{3^n}\right\rfloor</math> where {{math|1=''A'' ≈ 1.306377883863}} is [[Mills' constant]].

[[Alfred Aho|Aho]] and [[Neil Sloane|Sloane]] observed that in several important [[integer sequence]]s, each term is a constant plus the square of the previous term. They show that such sequences can be formed by rounding to the nearest integer the values of a double exponential function with middle exponent 2.<ref>{{citation|first1=A. V.|last1=Aho|author-link1=Alfred Aho|first2=N. J. A.|last2=Sloane|author-link2=N. J. A. Sloane|url=http://neilsloane.com/doc/doubly.html|title=Some doubly exponential sequences|journal=[[Fibonacci Quarterly]]|volume=11|year=1973|issue=4 |pages=429–437 |doi=10.1080/00150517.1973.12430815 }}.</ref>
Ionaşcu and Stănică describe some more general sufficient conditions for a sequence to be the floor of a double exponential sequence plus a constant.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ionaşcu | first1 = Eugen-Julien
 | last2 = Stănică | first2 = Pantelimon
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Acta Mathematica Universitatis Comenianae
 | pages = 75–87
 | title = Effective asymptotics for some nonlinear recurrences and almost doubly-exponential sequences
 | volume = LXXIII
 | url = http://faculty.nps.edu/pstanica/research/AMUC04.pdf
 | year = 2004}}.</ref>

==Applications==
===Algorithmic complexity===
In [[computational complexity theory]], [[2-EXPTIME]] is the class of decision problems solvable in double exponential time. It is equivalent to AEXPSPACE, the set of decision problems solvable by an [[alternating Turing machine]] in exponential space, and is a superset of [[EXPSPACE]].<ref>[[Christos Papadimitriou]], Computational Complexity (1994), {{isbn|978-0-201-53082-7}}. Section 20.1, corollary 3, page 495.</ref> An example of a problem in 2-EXPTIME that is not in EXPTIME is the problem of proving or disproving statements in [[Presburger arithmetic]].<ref>[[Michael J. Fischer|Fischer, M. J.]], and [[Michael O. Rabin]], 1974, "[http://www.lcs.mit.edu/publications/pubs/ps/MIT-LCS-TM-043.ps "Super-Exponential Complexity of Presburger Arithmetic.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060915010325/http://www.lcs.mit.edu/publications/pubs/ps/MIT-LCS-TM-043.ps |date=2006-09-15 }}" ''Proceedings of the SIAM-AMS Symposium in Applied Mathematics Vol. 7'': 27–41</ref>

In some other problems in the design and analysis of algorithms, double exponential sequences are used within the design of an algorithm rather than in its analysis. An example is [[Chan's algorithm]] for computing [[convex hull]]s, which performs a sequence of computations using test values {{math|1=''h''{{sub|''i''}} = 2{{sup|2{{sup|''i''}}}}}} (estimates for the eventual output size), taking time {{math|O(''n'' log ''h''{{sub|''i''}})}} for each test value in the sequence. Because of the double exponential growth of these test values, the time for each computation in the sequence grows singly exponentially as a function of {{mvar|i}}, and the total time is dominated by the time for the final step of the sequence. Thus, the overall time for the algorithm is {{math|O(''n'' log ''h'')}} where {{mvar|h}} is the actual output size.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Chan | first = T. M. | author-link = Timothy M. Chan
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02712873
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]
 | mr = 1414961
 | pages = 361–368
 | title = Optimal output-sensitive convex hull algorithms in two and three dimensions
 | volume = 16
 | year = 1996| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

In a different direction, Witteveen & Jeffery showed that any [[QMA]] protocol can be amplified (see [[BPP (complexity)|BPP]]) to have doubly-exponential error (with mild constraints on choice of gate sets).<ref>{{cite arXiv | last1=Jeffery | first1=Stacey | last2=Witteveen | first2=Freek | title=$&#123;\sf QMA&#125;=&#123;\sf QMA&#125;_1$ with an infinite counter | date=2025 | class=quant-ph | eprint=2506.15551 }}</ref>

===Number theory===
Some [[number theory|number theoretical]] bounds are double exponential. [[Odd perfect number]]s with {{mvar|n}} distinct prime factors are known to be at most <math>2^{4^n}</math>, a result of Nielsen (2003).<ref>{{citation
 | last = Nielsen | first = Pace P.
 | journal = INTEGERS: The Electronic Journal of Combinatorial Number Theory
 | pages = A14
 | title = An upper bound for odd perfect numbers
 | url = http://www.integers-ejcnt.org/vol3.html
 | volume = 3
 | year = 2003}}.</ref>

The maximal volume of a [[polytope]] in a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional [[integer lattice]] with {{math|''k'' ≥ 1}} [[Integer points in convex polyhedra|interior lattice points]] is at most
<math display="block">k\cdot(8d)^d\cdot15^{d\cdot2^{2d+1}},</math>
a result of Pikhurko (2001).<ref>{{citation|last=Pikhurko
 | first=Oleg
 | title=Lattice points in lattice polytopes
 | journal=[[Mathematika]]
 | volume=48
 | year=2001
 | issue=1–2
 | pages=15–24
 | arxiv=math/0008028
|bibcode = 2000math......8028P
 | doi=10.1112/s0025579300014339}}</ref>

The [[largest known prime number]] in the electronic era has grown roughly as a double exponential function of the year since [[J. C. P. Miller|Miller]] and [[David Wheeler (computer scientist)|Wheeler]] found a 79-digit prime on [[EDSAC]]1 in 1951.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Miller | first1 = J. C. P.
 | last2 = Wheeler | first2 = D. J.
 | doi = 10.1038/168838b0
 | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]
 |page=838
 | title = Large prime numbers
 | volume = 168
 | year = 1951
 | issue=4280|bibcode = 1951Natur.168..838M | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

===Theoretical biology===
{{one source section|date=February 2026}}
In [[population dynamics]] the growth of human population is sometimes supposed to be double exponential. Varfolomeyev and Gurevich<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Varfolomeyev | first1 = S. D.
 | last2 = Gurevich | first2 = K. G.
 | doi = 10.1006/jtbi.2001.2384
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal of Theoretical Biology
 | pages = 367–372
 | title = The hyperexponential growth of the human population on a macrohistorical scale
 | volume = 212
 | year = 2001
 | pmid = 11829357| bibcode = 2001JThBi.212..367V
 }}.</ref> experimentally fit

<math display="block">N(y)=375.6\cdot 1.00185^{1.00737^{y-1000}} \,</math>

where {{math|''N''(''y'')}} is the population in millions in year {{mvar|y}}.

===Physics===
In the [[Toda oscillator]] model of [[self-pulsation]], the logarithm of amplitude varies exponentially with time (for large amplitudes), thus the amplitude varies as double exponential function of time.<ref name="kouz">{{citation
 | last1 = Kouznetsov | first1 = D.
 | last2 = Bisson | first2 = J.-F.
 | last3 = Li | first3 = J.
 | last4 = Ueda | first4 = K.
 | doi = 10.1088/1751-8113/40/9/016
 | journal = [[Journal of Physics A]]
 | pages = 1–18
 | title = Self-pulsing laser as oscillator Toda: Approximation through elementary functions
 | url = http://www.iop.org/EJ/abstract/-search=15823442.1/1751-8121/40/9/016
 | volume = 40
 | year = 2007
 | issue = 9 | bibcode=2007JPhA...40.2107K| s2cid = 53330023
 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.535.5379
 }}.</ref>

Dendritic [[macromolecule]]s have been observed to grow in a doubly-exponential fashion.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Double Exponential Dendrimer Growth |first1=Tohru |last1=Kawaguchi |first2=Kathleen L. |last2=Walker |first3=Charles L. |last3=Wilkins |first4=Jeffrey S. |last4=Moore |journal=[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]] |year=1995 |volume=117 |number=8 |pages=2159–2165 |doi=10.1021/ja00113a005 |bibcode=1995JAChS.117.2159K }}</ref>
